The Tesseract

CountingLogicInvariants
Game: Build a four-dimensional cube step by step and turn it. Then take a little pair of arrows on a trip over its squares so that it comes home flipped over.
How to play: Press Start and keep pressing Continue. In the puzzle below, press the square buttons to move the coloured arrows. You win when they come back reversed.

The reper puzzle

Look for the math

A tesseract is the four-dimensional hypercube: all points (x, y, z, h) with every coordinate between 0 and 1. The picture is its shadow on the screen.

Counting its parts

Each step of the construction moves the last shape along a new direction. Every old part is then present twice, and every old part also sweeps out a new part one dimension higher. That doubling-plus-sweeping is exactly multiplication by 2x + 1, so the n-dimensional cube's parts are the coefficients of (2x + 1)n:

(2x + 1)4 = 16x4 + 32x3 + 24x2 + 8x + 1

Read from x4 down: 16 vertices, 32 edges, 24 squares, 8 cubes and 1 tesseract.

Turning in four dimensions

In 4D you turn about a plane, not a line, and there are six planes of rotation, one for each pair of axes. The cube drawn in colour can be turned through the fourth dimension until it shows its other side. A hyperplane Ax + By + Cz + Dh = E cuts the tesseract in a solid: a cube for h = 1/2, an octahedron for x + y + z + h = 2. The logic test checked both, and that every one of the six turns really is a rotation.

Coming home reversed

In a tesseract three squares meet at every edge. Glide the reper (without turning it) across the edge into the next square, then the next, and back into the first: it returns as a mirror image. Those three squares form a one-sided strip, like a Möbius strip. The logic test searched every route: three moves is the fewest from every square, the only three-move solutions go round one of the square's four edges, and no trip inside a single boundary cube can ever reverse the reper, because a cube's surface is two-sided.

Note the square's name, pick one of its edges, and visit the other two squares that share it.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
